1:
With his long discourse on the majesty of God now ended, Job pauses — and the witnesses gather first around that pause and the single word by which the historian reopens his mouth, mashal, a “parable.” The reformed John Gill pictures the scene: Job waited a while for Zophar, whose turn was next to reply, but neither he nor any of his friends resumed the debate; they kept a profound silence, either concluding him an obstinate man on whom no impression could be made, or being secretly convicted that he was right and they wrong, or simply surprised at the knowledge of divine things his last speech had shown. So, though they held their peace, Job did not, but “added to take up his parable,” as the words may be rendered.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the title. The discourse is called a mashal, the very word that heads Solomon’s proverbs, because it was grave and weighty and instructive, and Job spoke as one having authority; the word comes from a root signifying to rule or have dominion, and some think it intimates that Job now triumphed over his opponents and spoke as one who had baffled them — we say of an excellent preacher that he knows how dominari in concionibus, to command his hearers. A long strife had run between Job and his friends; and since an oath for confirmation is an end of strife, as Heb. 6:16 has it, Job now backs all he has said in defence of his integrity with a solemn oath.

The wesleyan-arminian voices agree on the tone. Adam Clarke derives meshalo from mashal, to exercise rule and dominion (Parkhurst), and grants that in this speech Job “assumes great boldness, exhibits his own unsullied character, and treats his friends with little ceremony”; John Wesley sums it as “his grave and weighty discourse.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott maps the whole remaining speech, now for the first time called a parable: his determination not to renounce his righteousness, his own estimate of the fate of the wicked, and the great hymn to wisdom that follows.

The latin-fathers voice of Gregory the Great reads the word more mystically, reflecting that in Holy Writ things of a mystical nature are often so mixed into the historical relation that obscurer particulars prick us, as with spurs, to look for a deeper sense beneath the plain one — the very naming of Job’s words as a “parable” inviting the reader to seek more than lies on the surface. The witnesses do not divide; together they mark the hinge, a silenced bench of friends and a man who, taking up his parable, binds his defence with an oath.
2:
The form of the oath opens on a phrase that has troubled the witnesses ever since — “As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment” — and they divide over whether it is reverent or rash. The reformed John Gill treats it first as a lawful and solemn oath, such as Jarchi marks it: a form used by God himself, who, because he can swear by no greater, swears by his own life; men too, when they must swear, should swear by the living God, in opposition to the lifeless idols of gold and silver and wood, and only in weighty cases, to end a strife that can be settled no other way than by an appeal to God — as was Job’s case, touching the integrity his friends impugned.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it “who hath deprived me of my right, and the Almighty who hath sorely saddened my soul,” and note how the speech is introduced as a continued lifting-up of his mashal, after the manner of Balaam’s oracles at Num. 23:7; the mashal is speech of an elevated, figurative tone, here the natural outgrowth of a solemn mood, like the Arab’s saying that “the proverb seals it.”

But over the clause “who hath taken away my judgment” the schools part. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as God turning aside his cause and refusing it a hearing, abandoning Job to the harsh judgment of his enemies — and he will not excuse the wording: “there appears a great want of reverence in these words”; Job speaks with an irritation, if not bitterness, that cannot be justified, and “no man should speak thus of his Maker.” The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the same oath, had already granted that Job here “speaks hardly of God, and unbecomingly,” a word for which Elihu would reprove him at ch. 34:5.

Against this severity the other voices hear faith, not blasphemy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds Job’s faith leading him to see that, though there be no explanation for his sufferings, they are yet laid on him by God for purposes of his own that are veiled from him; and John Wesley glosses the “who” gently — “though he knows my integrity, yet doth not plead my cause against my friends.” So the debate is genuine: is “who hath taken away my judgment” the murmur of a man momentarily despairing of justice, to be reproved, or the confession of a faith that submits to a providence it cannot read? The witnesses leave both readings standing over the oath.
3:
Job binds his oath to the whole remaining span of his life — “all the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils” — and the witnesses read the clause as both a limit and a reason. The reformed John Gill takes it plainly: so long as breath remained, the oath of God would lie upon him, and he bound himself under it for life. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the line as the parenthetical ground of the vow, “for still all my breath is in me, and the breath of Eloah in my nostrils” — Job swearing by the very life that is still within him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the doubled phrase a deliberate echo of man’s creation. Job alludes, he thinks, to the making of Adam, into whose nostrils God breathed the breath of life, so that the whole assertion may be a periphrasis for “as long as I live and have my understanding”; for nishmathi may be rendered “my mind” or “understanding,” and the ruach Eloah, the breath of God, is the principle of animal life, the same breathed into Adam at Gen. 2:7, by which he became a living and rational soul.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the oath, presses the moral latent in the words: that our resolutions against sin should be constant, resolutions for life; and that a reason for the vow lies hidden in it, since our breath will not be always in us. We must shortly breathe our last, and therefore, while breath is in us, we must never breathe out wickedness and deceit, nor say anything that will make against us when our breath departs. And the breath within us is called the spirit of God, Henry notes, because he breathed it into us — one more reason we must not use it to speak wickedness, for it is God who gives us life and breath, and while we have it we must praise him.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job pledges his integrity not for a moment but for the whole of a life he knows to be borrowed and fragile, held only so long as God’s breath is lent to his nostrils. What in Clarke’s hands becomes a meditation on the dust that Adam was, and in Henry’s a warning to spend the breath we have in praise and not in falsehood, is in all of them the same confession: that the man who swears by his own life swears by a thing not his own, and must answer for every word of it to the God who lent it.
4:
The matter of the oath is the honesty of Job’s own speech — that his lips shall not speak wickedness, nor his tongue utter deceit — and the witnesses weigh both what he swears and how absolutely he swears it. The reformed John Gill takes the wickedness Job forswears to include not merely a corrupt or idle word, nor evil spoken of his neighbours, but above all a lie against himself: he will not speak wickedly of his own soul by owning himself the wicked man and hypocrite his friends would have him confess. This is the very thing he swears he will never utter while any breath remains in him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch are careful about the mood of the words. The line is not to be rendered “my lips shall never speak what is false,” as though it were a fresh resolve made after the manner of a vow; it is rather the agreement of a confession Job has so often made already, and which remains unalterable, with the abiding fact. He does not so much promise future honesty as attest a present and settled truthfulness, sworn under the most solemn form.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the pledge of a consistent life: “as I have hitherto lived in all good conscience before God, as he knoweth, so will I continue to live” — the oath simply binding tomorrow to the integrity of every yesterday. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds it as a resolution against all lying whatsoever: Job would never maintain any doctrine, nor assert any matter of fact, but what he believed to be true, nor deny the truth however much it made against him.

Were he guilty, Henry adds, Job would not for all the world deny the charge, but would declare the whole truth and take to himself the shame of his hypocrisy; being innocent, he would as little betray his integrity by charging himself with what he never did. If we may not bear false witness against our neighbour, Henry says, then not against ourselves either. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job’s oath fences his tongue against a falsehood in both directions — against flattering his friends by a false confession, and against betraying his conscience by a false denial — and that this even-handed truthfulness is the ground on which the rest of his parable will stand.
5:
“God forbid that I should justify you” — Job’s recoil from his friends’ verdict is, the witnesses agree, a recoil not from their persons but from their doctrine. The reformed John Gill is careful to fence the words: Job does not take upon himself to judge their eternal state, for he counted them good men God-ward; what he could not justify was their censure of him, and their whole scheme of doctrine — that the wicked are always punished in this life and the good always prospered, and that a man may be read off as righteous or wicked by his outward circumstances. To approve such teaching would be to call evil good and good evil; to join in it would be, in the very sense of the word he uses, a profanation and a pollution, from which he shrinks with abhorrence.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the phrase on the argument: far be it from him that he should justify them by any confession of guilt. “You say that God afflicts me for my crimes; I say, and God knows it is truth, that I have not sinned so as to draw down any such judgment upon me. Your judgment, therefore, is pronounced at your own risk.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the logic simply: to admit the wickedness with which they charged him would be to justify them, to say that they were right and he was wrong, and this he resolves not to do.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, fixes the Hebrew of the vow beneath it: chalilah li is not a feminine form but a word of direction — “let it be a profanation to me” — so that Job swears that, until he expire, he will not put away his innocence, his tummah or purity of character; he will not cease from asserting it.

And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole as the explication of the oath: “God forbid that I should justify you in your uncharitable censures of me, by owning myself a hypocrite.” Job here thinks of dying and of getting ready for death, and therefore resolves never to part with his religion, though he had lost all he had in the world, and never to curse God as Satan, by his wife, had urged him at ch. 2:9. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the refusal not stubbornness but the fixed resolve of a man who will neither flatter his accusers nor betray his conscience by a lie against his own right.
6:
When Job cries that he holds fast his righteousness and will not let it go, the reformed John Gill steps in at once to say what righteousness he means. Not his personal or justifying righteousness before God, the righteousness of his own works — that, being convinced of its insufficiency, Job would no more hold fast than Paul would, who desired not to be found in his own righteousness at Phil. 3:9; nor even, here, the righteousness of his living Redeemer, though that too was his to plead. What he grips is the righteousness of his cause — the truth that it was for no wrong done to any man that God dealt thus with him. He had wronged none, had done justice to all; and this plea he would never let drop.

The wesleyan-arminian voices take the second clause, “my heart shall not reproach me.” Adam Clarke reads it as a resolve of life: “I stand firmly on this ground; I have endeavoured to live an upright life, and my afflictions are not the consequence of my sins”; and so to live henceforth that his conscience shall be void of offence, on the ground of 1 John 3:21, that if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God. John Wesley glosses the reproach precisely: Job’s heart shall not reproach him “with betraying my own cause and innocency” — the very surrender his friends were pressing on him would be the thing his conscience could not forgive.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the tense of the clause to a present, “my heart doth not reproach me for any of my days,” and Keil and Delitzsch read the same, taking the words as a partitive — his heart does not reproach him for so much as one of his days; the heart, they observe, standing here for the seat of self-knowledge, to which Job appeals as a witness no accusation can overrule.

Here a careful distinction runs through the witnesses without breaking into open dispute: Gill insists the righteousness held fast is not a claim to sinlessness before God but the justice of a particular cause, while Clarke and Henry hear in it the clear conscience of an honest life. Yet all converge on the one point, that Job’s grip on his integrity is not pride but the refusal of a clear conscience to accuse itself falsely; whatever he has lost, he will not, to buy his friends’ peace, let go the one thing he knows to be true.
7:
“Let mine enemy be as the wicked, and he that riseth up against me as the unrighteous” — the wish sounds like a curse, and the witnesses work to show what Job really means by it. The reformed John Gill reads it as the measure of Job’s abhorrence: so far was he from being the wicked man and hypocrite his friends supposed, that he would not be in the wicked man’s condition for all the world; if he might wish the worst evil he could conceive upon his bitterest enemy, he could wish him nothing worse than to be a wicked, unrighteous man — though in truth a good man cannot really wish even that, and the wish is needless, since the enemies of the godly, like his own Sabeans and Chaldeans, are wicked already.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a proverbial form, like the words to the king, “the dream be to those that hate thee,” at Dan. 4:19. Job so dreaded the very thought of being a hypocrite that, if he might wish the greatest evil to his worst enemy, he would wish him the portion of a wicked man, knowing that worse he could not wish him; we should all, Henry says, choose to be a beggar, an outlaw, a galley-slave, anything, rather than to be in the condition of the wicked, though clothed in all their pomp and outward prosperity. John Wesley agrees: “if I would wish to be revenged of my enemy, I could wish him no greater mischief than to be a wicked man.”

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, reads the line more forensically, as a wish not of moral horror but of vindication: “let my accuser be proved a lying and perjured man, because he has laid to my charge things which he cannot prove, and which are utterly false.” And the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a further nuance: while Job freely admits the wicked man is often prosperous, he declares he has no envy of him whatever, and would wish only his adversaries to share his lot.

So a small difference of reading opens here — whether “let mine enemy be as the wicked” is the cry that wickedness itself is the worst of fates, as Gill, Henry, and Wesley take it, or Clarke’s demand that his false accuser be exposed as the guilty one. Either way the verse serves Job’s purpose: to put the widest distance between himself and the wicked man whose doom he is now about to describe.
8:
“For what is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gained, when God taketh away his soul?” — and the witnesses divide first over who this doomed man is. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke protests that “hypocrite” most improperly translates the Hebrew chaneph, which means a polluted, profane wretch, a rascal or knave who sticks at nothing to gain his ends; here, a dishonest rogue who by cheating and overreaching has amassed a fortune. Could such a man have any well-grounded hope of eternal blessedness while he was acquiring his property by guilt and deceit? and of what avail is that property when his soul is summoned before the judgment-seat? — words, Clarke thinks, that were in our Lord’s eye when he asked what a man is profited if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul, at Matt. 16:26.

The reformed John Gill keeps the older sense of the hypocrite in religion, one who seems what he is not and does all to be seen of men; such a man may have a hope of the divine favour and of eternal happiness, but what will it signify, what will it issue in, at death? It is not like the believer’s hope, sure and steadfast and founded on the righteousness and sacrifice of Christ, but rests only on his outward substance, fancying that because God prospers him here he is high in his favour. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it to the same effect: “what is the hope of the godless, though he get him gain, when God taketh away his soul?”

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the verse in the mouth of a man agreeing, for once, with Bildad and Zophar, who had condemned the hypocrite’s hope at their own turns; the hypocrite is at once deceived and undeceived — he has gained, and on his gain he builds his hope, but God shall take away his soul, sorely against his will, as the rich fool’s was required of him at Luke 12:20, and then his hope will prove but vanity and a lie, standing him in no stead. John Wesley sums it: though they prosper in the world, God as the judge takes the soul away to be tried and determined to its everlasting state, and what will his hope be then?

The witnesses divide only on the word — polluted rogue or religious pretender — but agree on the ruin: a hope built on gain cannot survive the hand that takes the soul away, and the man who counted his prosperity a pledge of heaven finds it, at the last, no ransom at all.
9:
The next stroke of the argument is a question that expects the answer No — whether God will hear the wicked man’s cry when trouble at last comes upon him. The reformed John Gill answers flatly that he will not: God heareth not sinners who regard iniquity in their hearts, as the psalmist owns at Ps. 66:18; and though every man meets trouble in this life, it is at death and judgment that the wicked find sorrow, when, like the foolish virgins crying “Lord, Lord, open to us,” they cry for a mercy that will not come, and God laughs at their calamity, as at Prov. 1:26. Yet Gill is careful to add the other side of the truth: God does hear the cries of his own people in their trouble, and Job may reckon himself among those who call upon God and are answered.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in the run of rhetorical questions by which Job paints the godless man’s portion, joining it to the two that follow — will he delight himself in the Almighty? will he always call upon God? — a chain of interrogations whose force is that the hypocrite has neither the will nor the ground to pray.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the pastoral distinction the verse turns upon. If true repentance come upon the man, God will hear his cry and accept him, on the promise of Isa. 1:18; but if he continue impenitent and unchanged, let him not think to find favour. Trouble will certainly come — if not in life then in death, and surely in the judgment of the great day; and then he will cry, and pray, and pray earnestly, who in prosperity had slighted God or prayed coldly. But will God hear him then? In this life God has said he will not hear those who turn away their ear from his law; in the judgment to come it is certain the cry of those who lived and died in their hypocrisy will be unpitied and their pleas rejected, as with the foolish virgins shut out at Matt. 25:11.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the prayer of the finally impenitent, urgent as it grows under the lash of trouble, meets a heaven that has become, by his own long refusal, deaf to him — while the same God who will not hear the hypocrite’s cry is swift to hear the groan of a suffering saint like Job.
10:
The portrait deepens into a test of the heart: whether the hypocrite will delight himself in the Almighty and call upon God at all times. The reformed John Gill answers for the man’s whole inward disposition. He will not delight in God — not in his omnipotence, into whose hands it is a fearful thing to fall; not in his omniscience, that searches and knows the insincerity he hides from men; not in his holiness, which at heart he does not love; nor in God’s ways and worship, his word and ordinances and people, however fair a show he makes of it. The delight is feigned, and feigned delight cannot last.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the true worshipper’s language over against the false. Only the godly can say, “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire in comparison with thee,” as at Ps. 73:25, and can praise God’s name because it is comfortable; but this man has no such promise that he can plead, and therefore no assurance of access at all times to the presence of God. His religion has no inward sweetness, and so no perseverance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a diagnosis of unsound religion and its cause. Those are hypocrites who, though they profess religion, neither take pleasure in it nor persevere in it — who reckon it a task and a drudgery, use it only to serve a turn, and lay it aside when the turn is served; who will call upon God while it is in fashion or while the pang of devotion lasts, but leave it off when the hot fit is over. In prosperity such a man will not call upon God but slights him; in adversity he will not call upon God but is ready to curse him; he is weary of his religion the moment he gets nothing by it.

And the reason they do not persevere, Henry says, is that they have no delight in God: those who find no pleasure in the Almighty will not always call upon him, being easily inveigled by the pleasures of sense and easily run down by the crosses of life. The more comfort we find in our religion, he adds, the more closely we shall cleave to it. The witnesses do not divide; they make delight in God the very hinge of sincerity, the thing the hypocrite lacks and by whose lack he is at last known.
11:
Turning from the hypocrite to his hearers, Job offers to teach them — “I will teach you by the hand of God; that which is with the Almighty will I not conceal” — and the witnesses take up both the promise and the disputed phrase “by the hand of God.” The reformed John Gill reads the object of the teaching as the works and methods of God’s providence with wicked men and hypocrites: the wisdom of God in his dispensations, why he suffers such men to live in outward prosperity, and what in the issue will become of them. He renders the clause “concerning the hand of God,” with Broughton — not the works of nature Job had discoursed of before, but the more mysterious works of providence; and he notes that Job, a teacher and comforter of many in his prosperity, as ch. 4:3 recalls, was no less fit to teach now, adversity having been a school to him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads “by the hand of God” the other way, of the help by which Job teaches rather than the subject taught: relying on divine assistance, not speaking out of his own head, he will teach them the mind of the Almighty and conceal nothing, feeling the good hand of his God upon him — as the Chaldee has it, “by the prophecy of God.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott holds the two senses side by side, rendering it either “I will teach you of the hand of God” or “what is in the power of God.”

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into the great turn of Job’s argument. Job agreed with his friends that wicked people are miserable and that God will surely reckon with cruel oppressors — this truth the angry disputants all confessed; where he differed was in their haste, for they held the deserved judgments fall presently and visibly, while Job held that vengeance often strikes slowly, yet strikes surely and severely, and that reprieves are no pardons. So he undertakes to set the matter in a true light: what he would teach is “that which is with the Almighty,” the counsels of God concerning the wicked which are hidden with him and not to be hastily judged; and he would teach it by God’s strength and assistance, for those whom God teaches with a strong hand, as at Isa. 8:11, are best able to teach others.

The witnesses divide gently over the preposition — the hand that helps him teach, or the hand of God that is his theme — but agree on the substance, that Job now claims to speak not against the friends’ creed but against their impatient misuse of it: the wicked man’s doom is real, but it is not the swift and legible thing they had made it, and therefore his own affliction is no proof against him.
12:
Job appeals to his hearers’ own eyes — “Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it” — and the witnesses find in this verse the key to everything that follows. The reformed John Gill takes the seeing plainly: men of observation as they were, the friends must have seen the wicked spreading himself like a green bay tree, as at Ps. 37:35, and hypocrites in flourishing circumstances, and good men bowed under affliction — Job himself an instance before their very eyes.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch call this verse of the greatest importance for interpreting all that comes after. When Job says “ye yourselves — every one of you — have beheld it all,” he grants what he had hitherto seemed to deny, that the lot of the evil-doer, as a rule though not without exceptions, is indeed such as the friends have described. What he denies is their application of it: “wherefore then are ye vain in vanity?” — blinded by self-delusion in fastening that lot upon him, who does not bear the marks of a wicked man. The verb, they note, is the same used of Israel’s becoming vain after idols, and echoed where Rom. 1:21 says men became vain in their imaginations.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the reproach. Adam Clarke renders the emphatic Hebrew “why then should ye babble babblings,” or, as he coins it, “vanitize vanity”; John Wesley reads it as an appeal to shared experience — “I speak what is confirmed by your own, as well as others’, experience” — and takes the vanity to be their condemning him for a wicked man merely because he is afflicted. The fault, on Wesley’s reading, lies not in the doctrine but in the verdict: they have turned a true observation into a false sentence, making Job’s suffering the proof of a guilt it cannot prove.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott alone turns the clause a different way, referring “ye have seen it” not to the fate of the wicked but to Job’s own witness: “you have seen me so proclaim the great power of God.” So the schools part slightly over what the friends have seen — the notorious spectacle of the wicked man’s end, as most of the witnesses hold, or, with Ellicott, Job’s own proclaiming of God’s power. But on the sting they agree: whatever the friends have seen with their eyes, they have misread with their judgment, and their vanity lies not in the fact but in the false inference they draw from it against Job.
13:
“This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, which they shall receive of the Almighty” — with this solemn heading, borrowed almost word for word from Zophar’s own conclusion at ch. 20:29, Job opens the great description that fills the rest of the chapter, and the witnesses raise at once the question that has vexed it ever since: are these his own words, or another’s? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott records the boldest theory — that some have thought the remainder of the chapter, and perhaps the next as well, to be the missing third speech of Zophar, the rubric “Then answered Zophar the Naamathite” having dropped from the text. Yet whatever is gained in symmetry, Ellicott judges, is lost in dramatic effect; Bildad had little to say and Zophar nothing more, so that Job was left virtually master of the field. He thinks it likelier that Job himself speaks, willing to show how completely he accepts the facts of his friends while refusing their inference — quite ready to allow that the prosperity of the wicked is seeming rather than real, and must eventually come to nought.

On the substance the schools converge but shade the timing differently. The reformed John Gill insists the portion here described is not chiefly in this life but after death: banishment from the presence of God, the second death, a portion with the hypocrites of Matt. 24:51 — for the wicked man’s true portion is “with God,” appointed by him, however he may prosper in the world. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a mixed dispensation: God does not always show his displeasure by reducing the wicked to poverty and affliction, though he often does so that men may see it; at other times he seems to pass them by, reserving their judgment for another world.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, simply renders the verse as the title of the doom that follows. So the witnesses hold together a genuine debate on two fronts: whether the passage is Job’s own teaching or a stray speech of Zophar’s — with Ellicott and the rest keeping it Job’s own — and whether the wicked man’s portion falls visibly in this life, is reserved for the world to come, or is paid out in both. What none of them doubts is that Job speaks it to press home his one contention: that a man may share this portion in the end without wearing the marks of it now, so that his own affliction proves nothing against him.
14:
The description begins with the wicked man’s children, and the witnesses read the multiplying of his house as a blessing turned to a curse. The reformed John Gill notes that a numerous offspring is an external good common to bad men and good — proud Haman left ten sons, and wicked Ahab seventy — so that many children is no sure sign of God’s favour. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that though a large family was reckoned a benediction of the Almighty, it is not always so; the offspring of the wicked are partly cut off by violent deaths and partly reduced to great poverty, so that the very fruitfulness he gloried in becomes the field on which his ruin is reaped.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet starkly — “if his children multiply, it is for the sword, and his offspring have not bread enough” — the more children he leaves and the greater the estate he leaves them in, the more and fairer the marks he sets up for the arrows of God’s judgment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out that thought at length, ranging the three sore judgments of 2 Sam. 24:13 — sword, famine, and pestilence — against the wicked man’s seed. Some of his children shall die by the sword: the sword of war, for those who are bred to live by the sword, like Esau at Gen. 27:40, commonly die by it; or the sword of justice for their crimes, or of the murderer for their estates. Others shall die by famine, their father having thought to secure them large estates, yet they are so reduced that they have not a competency of bread, or so discontented that what they have does not satisfy — so straitened, Henry adds, that they eat and yet have not enough, the word of Hag. 1:6 coming true upon them. And those that remain shall be buried in death — that is, swept off by the plague — and buried privately and in haste, without solemnity or mourning.

So the parents who hoped to live on in their children, and to be honoured in their preferment, leave instead only the more numerous prey for the sword, the famine, and the pestilence. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the fullest quiver may become, in the wicked man’s hand, only the fuller measure of his sorrow, and that the offspring he counted his security are the surest mark of his doom.
15:
The wicked man’s survivors fare no better than his slain, and the witnesses fasten on the grim phrase “buried in death” and the widows who do not weep. The reformed John Gill takes “those that remain” as those left after his death, or who have escaped the sword and famine already named, now overtaken by a further stroke. The wesleyan-arminian voices read the burial as an utter and remediless destruction: Adam Clarke, keeping the literal “buried in death,” finds in it that death itself shall be the place where such a man lies, with no redemption and no resurrection to life; and the widows do not weep because the public will not bewail him — for when the wicked perish there is shouting, as at Prov. 11:10. The word for those that remain, Clarke observes, is seridaiv, his remains, whether the man himself or his household. John Wesley makes the widows plural by the man’s polygamy, and reads their tearlessness as relief: they too had groaned under his tyranny, and rejoice to be delivered from it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear a subtler note. The women he leaves do not celebrate the usual mourning rites, such as those over Sarah at Gen. 23:2, not because they are glad but because the decreed punishment, stroke upon stroke robbing them of husband and children, prevents all observance of the customs of grief, and the sheer shock stifles the very feeling of pity. The verse, they add, is common to our poet and the psalm of Asaph at Ps. 78:64, where the widows likewise made no lamentation.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, reads the death as obscure, exciting no sympathy — their very dying is as a burial, consigning them to oblivion — and takes “his widows” either as those women commonly hired to make lamentation, who here have none to hire them, or as the widows of the survivors themselves.

So the witnesses differ over why the widows do not weep — whether from relief at a tyrant’s fall, as Clarke and Wesley have it, or from a grief too stunned and overwhelmed to keep the forms of mourning, as Keil and Delitzsch prefer — and over who the “widows” are, the man’s many wives or the hired mourners of Ellicott’s reading. But all agree on the desolation the verse pictures: a death so heavy with judgment that even the tears which attend the meanest funeral are dried up at his.
16:
From his children the description turns to the wicked man’s treasure, heaped up, as the verse says, “as the dust,” and his raiment “prepared as the clay.” The reformed John Gill reads the images as a portrait of the man’s very soul: to heap silver like dust denotes not only the abundance he gathers but the bias of a mind that cannot be content without amassing it, and his diligence and success in the gathering; the very heaping betrays a heart that measures its safety by its hoard. The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the vanity of it. Adam Clarke observes that though he amass riches in the greatest abundance he shall not enjoy them, for unsanctified wealth is a curse to its possessor; money, of all earthly possessions the most dangerous, is the readiest agent of good or evil, so that he who perverts it is doubly cursed and he who uses it aright doubly blessed; for almost every kind of want may be speedily relieved by money rightly used, while he who abuses it can sin more in an hour through it than in a week by any other means. John Wesley notes only that “as clay” means in great abundance, the man’s garments as plentiful as heaps of mire.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the comparison in its full force: dust and the dirt of the streets are, as at Zech. 9:3, the emblem of an abundance so great that it cheapens even what is precious — the man has silver as common as dust and clothing as common as clay.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees in the heaping the whole care and business of worldly men, who lade themselves with thick clay, as at Hab. 2:6, and gather until the silver is cankered and the garments moth-eaten, as Jas. 5:2 warns. But what comes of it? He shall never be the better for it himself; death will strip him and rob him, if he be not stripped sooner.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the wicked man’s wealth, gathered like dust and clay and grown as worthless as they, is heaped only to be left — and, as the next verse will show, left to hands he never meant to enrich. The very abundance that seemed the proof of his prospering is, in the witnesses’ reading, but the measure of how much he must one day let go.
17:
What the wicked man gathers, another wears — “he may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver” — and the witnesses dwell on this quiet reversal of providence. The reformed John Gill notes only, on the wording, that the verse begins with the raiment mentioned last in the couplet before, a turn frequent in the Hebrew and eastern tongues: such things a wicked man may indeed prepare, and often does, but the enjoying of them is not his, the wearing and the dividing falling to another.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the theology of it. Money is God’s own property — “the silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the Lord,” at Hag. 2:8 — and though it be abused for a time in unrighteous hands, God in the course of his providence brings it back to its proper use, so that often the righteous possess the inheritance of the wicked.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the same providence most fully. God will so order it that the just shall wear the wicked man’s raiment and the innocent divide his silver; for the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just, as Prov. 13:22 says, and God disposes of men’s estates as he pleases, often making their wills against their wills. The just whom the wicked hated and persecuted shall have rule over all his labour and recover with interest what was violently taken; the Egyptians’ jewels were the Israelites’ pay, and, as Solomon observes at Eccl. 2:26, God makes the sinner a drudge to gather and heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God.

Nor will the innocent hoard it as the gatherer did, Henry adds, but divide it to the poor, giving a portion to seven and to eight; for money is like manure, good for nothing unless it be spread, and he that by unjust gain increases his substance does but gather it for one who will pity the poor, as at Prov. 28:8. And when God enriches good men, Henry reminds us, they are but stewards, and must give account: what bad men bring a curse upon their families by ill-getting, good men bring a blessing upon theirs by the well-using. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the sweetest irony of the wicked man’s portion, that his very hoarding becomes, in God’s hand, the provision of the righteous he despised.
18:
The wicked man’s house is as frail as his wealth is fleeting, and the witnesses turn over the double image of the moth and the watchman’s booth. The reformed John Gill reads the first of the moth that builds its dwelling within a garment by eating into and destroying it, only to be shaken or brushed out; so the wicked man rears himself a stately palace and looks for it to stand for ever, but, building it with the mammon of unrighteousness and with what is due to others, he brings ruin on himself and his house, which he and his posterity enjoy but a little while. The figure, Gill adds, fits the hypocrite’s hope no less than his house — a spider’s web, a moth-eaten garment, a house upon the sand.

The wesleyan-arminian voices draw the picture from life. Adam Clarke takes the moth’s house rather of the frail case the insect spins for itself in its caterpillar state, a temporary lodging soon dissolved during its change into a winged thing; and the “booth that the keeper maketh” he explains as the slight shed the watchman of a vineyard throws up to shade him while the grapes ripen, built of the lightest and most worthless materials and left, after the vintage, to be dissolved by the winter rains. John Wesley reads both figures the same way — the moth that settles in a garment but is quickly dispossessed and crushed, the booth the keeper suddenly rears in fruit-time and as quickly pulls down again.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet “he hath built as a moth his house, and as a hut that a watchman setteth up,” and press the comparison home: the house of the ungodly man, though it be a palace, is as brittle and perishable a thing, and as easily destroyed, as the fine spinning of a moth. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds the note of false security: the man is as much at ease in his house as a moth in its garment, with no apprehension of danger, yet it will prove of no longer continuance than the keeper’s booth, quickly taken down and gone, so that his place shall know him no more.

So the witnesses differ only on the insect’s craft — whether the house is likened to the moth’s fragile tunnel in the cloth, as most take it, or to the cocoon of its brief larval life, as Clarke prefers — and agree that the wicked man builds for permanence what is fashioned, from the very first, for ruin.
19:
“The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered; he openeth his eyes, and he is not” — a verse of many readings, over which the witnesses divide more than anywhere in the chapter. The reformed John Gill offers two senses: either the wicked rich man lies down on his bed but cannot be gathered to rest, the abundance and the fear of losing it robbing him of sleep; or he lies down while his wealth “is not gathered” — not yet taken from him — and wakes to find it suddenly gone.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads “lie down” of the grave: the rich man is not gathered, having neither a respectable burial among men nor a place with the righteous in the kingdom of God, and “openeth his eyes” at the resurrection morning only to find that “he is not,” utterly and for ever lost. Yet Clarke offers too the picture nearest Job’s own case — the man lying down secure that his property is safe, who opens his eyes at dawn to find that marauders in the night have stripped him of all, as the Sabeans stripped Job. John Wesley reads “lie down in death,” the man denied honourable interment, his carcase lying like dung upon the earth, gone in the twinkling of an eye as though he had never been, his very name extinct with him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes the “gathering” of the wealth: “he openeth his eyes, and it” — his riches — “is not”; or else, as soon as he opens his eyes hoping to enjoy them, he himself is suddenly cut off. Keil and Delitzsch keep the terse Hebrew, “he lieth down rich and doeth it not again, he openeth his eyes and is no more.” And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the restless conscience beneath the wealth: the rich man lies down as in a strong city, bidding his soul take its ease, but he shall not be gathered — his mind never composed or settled to enjoy his abundance, full of tossings till the dawn, when he opens his eyes and finds himself and all he has hastening away.

So the readings genuinely diverge — whether the man is denied burial, or robbed of his goods, or robbed only of his rest — yet all the witnesses meet in the swiftness of the end: he shuts his eyes rich and opens them to find himself, or his all, gone in a moment.
20:
The description now sweeps toward the wicked man’s end, and the witnesses feel the rising flood of it — “terrors take hold on him as waters; a tempest stealeth him away in the night.” The reformed John Gill hears in the terrors both the dread of death, the king of terrors, and the terrors that seize the guilty soul after death: the accusations of an awakened conscience, the curses of the law, the poured-out wrath of the Almighty. They come as waters, like a flood, a terror on every side — a very Magor-missabib, the name Jeremiah was given at Jer. 20:3 — rolling in with an irresistible force and without ceasing, wave following wave, so that he is beset behind and before and can find no way of escape.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the same violence. Adam Clarke reads the terrors as an irresistible flood, the man overwhelmed by a tempest in the night, when darkness half hides his danger and cuts off all way of escape. John Wesley traces the terror to the sense of approaching death or judgment, coming as violently as a river bursting its banks, God’s wrath falling like a tempest and, withal, unexpectedly, like a thief in the night.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet “terrors take hold of him as a flood; by night a tempest stealeth him away,” setting the whirlwind of judgment over the false security of the verses before. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the terrors into a study of the two despairs a dying wicked man may fall to: either a silent, sullen despair, in which the tempest of God’s wrath may be said to steal him away in the night, when none takes notice; or an open, clamorous despair, in which he is carried off and hurled from his place as with a storm. The very sickness, Henry notes, is mingled with sorrow and wrath, as Solomon says at Eccl. 5:17.

Death, Henry says, is to a godly man like a fair gale of wind to convey him to the heavenly country, but to a wicked man like an east wind, a tempest that hurries him away in confusion and amazement to destruction. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the terrors which the man kept at bay while his wealth lay about him break in at the last like a night-flood, and sweep him, unready, out of the world.
21:
The tempest of the previous verse is now named — the east wind — and the witnesses attend to the peculiar terror of that wind in the East. The reformed John Gill takes it of a wind strong and powerful, carrying all before it, an image to which afflictions are elsewhere likened, as at Jer. 18:17; here it is death, armed with the wrath of God, hurrying the wicked man out of the world against his will, from house and family and estate, to his place among the devils. The Septuagint and Vulgate, Gill notes, render it “a burning wind,” such as travellers describe in those countries, which catches a man up so suddenly that he has time only to cry “I burn” before he drops dead; and so the wicked man, who had braved every lesser blast, is caught up in this one and is gone.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the wind its full natural history. The qadim that comes from the Arabian desert is the destructive, devastating, parching wind above all others; rare in summer, more frequent in winter and early spring, it scorches the tender vegetation and brings a year of famine, so that it earned the name of the “devastating wind.” It is dry, they add, and excites the blood, contracts the chest, and breeds restlessness and anxiety and sleepless nights, till man and beast alike feel sickly under it — whence whatever is unpleasant and revolting in life came to be compared to the east wind. So violent is it that in the Lebanon it took the name of the devastating wind, and both man and beast feel weak and sickly while it prevails.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the picture short and sharp. Adam Clarke identifies it with the “levanter,” the euroclydon, the very eastern storm that wrecked Paul at Acts 27:14; John Wesley reads it as some terrible judgment, most vehement and pernicious, carrying the man out of the palace where he had thought to dwell for ever, borne off by an enemy or by death.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the wind which in that land withered the harvest and sickened the living is the fit emblem of the stroke that lifts the wicked man bodily from his place and is gone with him before he can resist — the very security of his palace turned, in a night, into the thing from which he is swept.
22:
As the storm reaches its height, the verse turns to the one who drives it — “for God shall cast upon him, and not spare; he would fain flee out of his hand” — and the witnesses divide over who, or what, is the hurler. The reformed John Gill reads it plainly of God, who casts upon the wicked man his own sins, and wrath, and deserved punishment, like a talent of lead, and that without any mercy at all; for though the wicked have much sparing mercy in this world, they have none in the next — the God who spared not the angels that sinned, nor the old world, nor Sodom, as 2 Pet. 2:4 recalls, will not spare them. John Wesley reads the same, of God casting his darts or plagues one after another, while the man would flee from the judgments of God but in vain.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, keeps the subject the storm of the verses before: it is the tempest that shall incessantly pelt him and give him no respite, nor can he by any means escape its fury. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers yet a third hand: the Authorized Version supplies “God” as the subject, but good sense arises, he thinks, from understanding it of the man whom the wicked oppressor had wronged, who now, glad of the chance to avenge himself, casts upon him and will not spare. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received reading, rendering it “God casteth upon him without sparing; before his hand he fleeth utterly away.”

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds that received sense most fully: while the man lived he had the benefit of sparing mercy, but now the day of God’s patience is over, and what God casts down there is no flying from nor bearing up under — God who cast great stones from heaven on the Canaanites at Josh. 10:11, and casts down his anger in its full weight like the talent of lead of Zech. 5:7. The damned sinner would fain flee out of his hand, but the gates are barred; those who will not now flee to the arms of divine grace will not be able to flee from the arms of divine wrath.

So the witnesses genuinely divide over the subject — God, or the storm, or the avenging victim — yet agree that whoever’s hand it is, it falls without pity and cannot be escaped; the wicked man who had so long fled the reckoning is at last overtaken by a hand from which there is no flight.
23:
“Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place” — the chapter ends on a gesture of derision, and the witnesses divide over whose hands they are. The reformed John Gill reads the clapping as an act of joy and triumph, of scorn and derision — done at the wicked man’s death, or hereafter while the wrath of God is poured upon him, and done by righteous men, not from any evil passion, but rejoicing in the glory of the divine justice displayed in his destruction. The verb, Gill notes, may be rendered impersonally, “hands shall be clapped at him,” so as to take in angels and saints together, all heaven approving and applauding the just procedure of God against the wicked.

The wesleyan-arminian voices agree on the derision but not on the hand. John Wesley takes it of men clapping in joy at the removal of such a public pest, and in astonishment, contempt, and scorn, and hissing him out in detestation. But Adam Clarke insists that these two closing verses belong to the storm, so that the word “men” should be dropped as “God” was in the verse before: it is the tempest that shall clap its hands against him, and hiss — or shriek — him out of his place, the storm personified, and the wicked actor hissed off the stage of the world. Clarke recalls the ancient custom of clapping and hissing an unworthy man out of public office, as the crowds of Europe still hiss a displeasing figure to this day.

So the witnesses close the chapter on a small but real division — whether the hands that clap and the mouths that hiss are those of righteous men and applauding angels, as Gill and Wesley have it, rejoicing in God’s justice, or, as Clarke would have it, the very storm of judgment driving the man from his place.

Either way the note is the same on which the whole description has moved: the wicked man, for all his children and silver and stately house, is swept off at last amid a universal derision, his place glad to be rid of him. And with that verdict Job rests his parable — having granted his friends every fact of the wicked man’s doom, and taken from them only the false inference that such a doom was written over his own afflicted head.
